Well, doctor, it's... it's just been a really, really difficult time lately. You see, my dear friend from choir—we've sat next to each other in the alto section for, oh, it has to be fifteen years now—she passed away. And it was just so sudden, you know? One Sunday she's there handing out the sheet music and asking about my grandkids, and the next... well, she's just gone. 

And ever since she passed so suddenly, I just... I haven't been myself at all. I really haven't. It's the strangest thing, but I find myself getting so upset over things that shouldn't be a big deal. Like, I'll just sit at the kitchen table and cry over the potluck lists! I was looking at the sign-up sheet for the Sunday luncheon the other day, and I just broke down weeping. And I get all worked up about phone calls that I used to handle so easy. People will call the house to ask about the church bulletin or the usher schedule, things I've managed with my eyes closed for years, and I just get entirely flustered and worked up over picking up the receiver. 

I've even started missing the church planning things... the committee meetings and the charity drives and such. I never, ever miss those. I've helped plan the church calendar since my kids were in high school, but lately I just stay home. I just don't know what's wrong with me, but I can't seem to keep it together like I used to.

Well, no, not really. I mean, I try, I really do try. Like my gardening, for instance. I have a lovely little patch of roses out back—mostly floribundas, though I do have a beautiful climbing rose on the trellis that my husband put up before he passed. Usually, I'd be out there every morning, rain or shine, deadheading and checking for aphids. I always found it so peaceful, you know? Just me and the birds and the dirt. But lately... well, I'll go out there with my shears, and I just stand there looking at them. I'll clip one or two stems, and then I just feel this heavy sigh come over me, and I put the shears right back in the bucket and go inside. It just doesn't bring me that little spark of joy it usually does. 

And it's the same with my baking. I've always been the one to bake the communion bread—the recipe with the honey and the whole wheat, everyone says it's much better than those little wafers. I usually love the whole process, the kneading and the rising, the smell filling up the kitchen. But last week, when it was my turn, I just bought a couple of loaves from the bakery down the street. I couldn't even bring myself to pull the flour out of the pantry. I just sat in the kitchen staring at the mixing bowl, feeling completely empty. It's like all the color has just drained out of everything I used to love doing. I just don't have the heart for any of it right now.

Guilty? Oh, goodness, no... no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I know sometimes people get all tangled up in knots when someone passes, thinking, oh, I should have called more, or I should have noticed something was wrong, or maybe they had a fight they never resolved. But with us... well, we saw each other just about every single week. Every Sunday for service, and Wednesdays for practice, regular as clockwork. 

The very last time I saw her, right before it happened, we were just standing by the fellowship hall coffee urn, and she was telling me all about her granddaughter's upcoming recital—she plays the flute, you know, such a sweet, talented little girl—and she looked perfectly fine. Not a care in the world. And then... well, her daughter told me it was just peaceful, in her sleep. Her heart just stopped. So there wasn't anything anyone could have done. It wasn't like she was laid up in the hospital and I forgot to visit, or we'd had some silly falling out. We never, ever argued. Not in fifteen years! Except maybe once, oh, years and years ago, over whether to use the blue hymnals or the red ones for the Christmas Eve service, but that was just us being silly. 

So, no, I don't have any guilt weighing on my heart. I know I was a good friend to her and she was a wonderful friend to me. It's really just the... the sheer shock of it all. Just the absolute suddenness that I can't seem to wrap my head around. You just don't expect to be drinking coffee with someone one day and then... well, you just don't expect them to be gone. But no, no guilt. Just this awful, heavy sadness that won't lift.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Oh, goodness, pleasure... well, I suppose that’s really what we were just talking about, isn't it? The gardening and the baking, those were my main things. And like I said, those are just completely gone for me right now. I just can't seem to muster up the energy or the... the joy for them. 

Let me think... is there anything else? Well, there's my evening television programs. Usually, I love watching those British mysteries, you know the ones, where it's a cozy little village and everyone knows everyone else's business, but then there's a murder and the local vicar or some little old lady has to solve it. My husband and I used to watch them together, and I kept the tradition going. I usually find them so comforting, trying to piece together the clues before the detective does. But lately... well, I turn the television on, right at eight o'clock, just like always. I sit in my usual chair with my cup of chamomile tea, and I look at the screen, but I'm not really watching it. The characters are talking, and I know they're solving a mystery, but I just can't follow the plot. My mind just wanders off, thinking about her, or just thinking about nothing at all, really. Just this sort of blank, heavy feeling. Before I know it, the hour is up, they've caught the killer, and I couldn't even tell you who it was or why they did it. 

And then there's the church choir, of course. Singing has always been such a huge part of my life. I'm a soprano, well, a second soprano these days, the high notes aren't quite what they used to be when I was in my thirties. But usually, Wednesday night practice is the highlight of my week. I love the harmonies, I love the fellowship, I love the way the music fills up the sanctuary. But since she passed... I haven't been back. I just can't bring myself to walk through those doors and see her empty spot in the alto section. She always stood right behind me, second row on the left. Sometimes she'd tap me on the shoulder if we were supposed to stand and I hadn't noticed the director's cue. So, no, I haven't been singing either. 

I suppose the long and short of it is... no. No, doctor, I really can't think of a single thing that I'm actually finding pleasure in right now. I just go through the motions of the day, making my meals, washing the dishes, checking the mail, but it's all just... flat. Everything is just so flat and gray. It's like I'm just waiting for the day to be over so I can go to sleep, but then I wake up the next morning and it's just the same flat, gray routine all over again. I just don't know how to get the color back into things.

Well, yes. Yes, I suppose I have been. It's just... ever since my choir friend passed so suddenly, I really just haven't been myself at all. 

Take the church planning committee, for example. We meet on the second Tuesday of every month, usually in the fellowship hall, to go over the calendar and organize the upcoming events. I've been on that committee for, oh, it must be twelve years now, and I've started missing those meetings. I just can't bring myself to go, which is so unlike me—I never, ever would have missed those church planning things before. I was always the one leading the charge, making sure everything was running smoothly! 

But now... well, the other day I was trying to look over the potluck sign-up sheets for the upcoming spring luncheon. Usually I love organizing that, making sure everyone is assigned a proper dish so we don't end up with five potato salads and absolutely no desserts. But I was just sitting there at my kitchen table, looking at the names, and I just started crying. Just weeping right over the potluck lists! It makes absolutely no sense, but the tears just wouldn't stop. 

And the phone calls, too. I used to handle all those coordination calls so easily, you know, people calling to ask if they should bring paper plates or if they need to come early to set up the folding chairs. It was second nature to me, I could chat and organize all afternoon. But now, the phone rings and I just get all worked up. My chest gets tight and I just stare at the caller ID until the answering machine finally picks up. I can't even bring myself to pick up the receiver to talk to people I've known for decades. So I just stay home. I stay home and I ignore the calls and I skip the meetings, because I just... I just can't face anyone right now. I don't even recognize myself behaving this way, hiding away from everyone, but I just don't have it in me to go out and pretend everything is normal.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Avoiding places that remind me of her? Hmm... well, I'm not sure I'd say that, exactly. I know I mentioned the choir room earlier, and not wanting to see her empty spot in the alto section, but... outside of that, I haven't really noticed myself doing that. I mean, it's not like I'm purposely staying away from the places we used to go together just because they bring up memories. 

Like the little garden center down on Route 4, for instance. We used to go there every single spring to pick out our flats of impatiens and petunias. She always took so long deciding between the pinks and the purples, and I'd just be standing there with my cart, teasing her, telling her they all look exactly the same once they're in the ground! She was so particular about her flower beds. But I wouldn't avoid going to that nursery now just because it reminds me of her. If anything, those memories are quite dear to me. 

The truth is, I'm just... I'm just not going anywhere at all. It's not the memories keeping me away from places, it's just this heavy feeling I have about absolutely everything. Like I was saying about the phone calls, I'm ignoring everybody, even people who didn't know her from Adam. The girl who does my hair, Betty, she called on Tuesday to remind me of my regular trim, and I just let it ring and ring. Betty didn't even know her, they never even crossed paths. And the mailman, I usually wave or say hello when he drops the letters in the box, but lately I just wait until his truck turns the corner before I even open the front door. 

So, no, doctor, I don't think I'm running away from reminders of my friend. I think I'm just... well, I'm just sort of retreating from the whole world right now. Does that make sense? It's just too much trouble to put on a brave face and make small talk, no matter where I am or who I'm with, whether they remind me of her or not.

Alone? Well, I suppose that depends on how you look at it. I am at home, yes, I'm at home all day long, every single day. But I'm not entirely by myself, because my husband is there. Constantly? Wishing she were here? Well... no, I wouldn't say constantly. It’s a strange thing, isn't it? You'd think I would be. You'd think I'd be sitting there in my chair replaying all our old conversations or crying over photographs, just wishing she could walk through the front door and tell me all about what her grandchildren are up to. I wasn't really thinking about anything at all. 

It's just this terrible flatness. So, no, I'm not consumed with thoughts of her every waking second. It's not this sharp, piercing pain of missing her all day long, it's more like... well, like all the color has just been washed out of the room, and it takes entirely too much effort to even form a thought about why. Does that make sense? I just feel so completely drained that I don't even have the energy to actively wish for things to be different anymore. I'm just sitting there, letting the clock tick.

Not a care in the world. And then... well, her daughter told me it was just peaceful, in her sleep. Her heart just stopped. So there wasn't anything anyone could have done. It wasn't like she was laid up in the hospital and I forgot to visit, or we'd had some silly falling out. We never, ever argued. Not in fifteen years! Except maybe once, oh, years and years ago, over whether to use the blue hymnals or the red ones for the Christmas Eve service, but that was just us being silly. \n\nSo, no, I don't have any guilt weighing on my heart. I know I was a good friend to her and she was a wonderful friend to me. It's really just the... the sheer shock of it all. Just the absolute suddenness that I can't seem to wrap my head around. You just don't expect to be drinking coffee with someone one day and then... well, you just don't expect them to be gone. But no, no guilt. Just this awful, heavy sadness that won't lift.\n\nDoctor: Are there any activities that you still find pleasure in since your friend passed away?\n\nPatient: Oh, goodness, pleasure... well, I suppose that’s really what we were just talking about, isn't it? The gardening and the baking, those were my main things. And like I said, those are just completely gone for me right now. I just can't seem to muster up the energy or the... the joy for them. \n\nLet me think... is there anything else? Well, there's my evening television programs. Usually, I love watching those British mysteries, you know the ones, where it's a cozy little village and everyone knows everyone else's business, but then there's a murder and the local vicar or some little old lady has to solve it. My husband and I used to watch them together, and I kept the tradition going. I usually find them so comforting, trying to piece together the clues before the detective does. But lately... well, I turn the television on, right at eight o'clock, just like always. I sit in my usual chair with my cup of chamomile tea, and I look at the screen, but I'm not really watching it. The characters are talking, and I know they're solving a mystery, but I just can't follow the plot. My mind just wanders off, thinking about her, or just thinking about nothing at all, really. Just this sort of blank, heavy feeling. Before I know it, the hour is up, they've caught the killer, and I couldn't even tell you who it was or why they did it. \n\nAnd then there's the church choir, of course. Singing has always been such a huge part of my life. I'm a soprano, well, a second soprano these days, the high notes aren't quite what they used to be when I was in my thirties. But usually, Wednesday night practice is the highlight of my week. I love the harmonies, I love the fellowship, I love the way the music fills up the sanctuary. But since she passed... I haven't been back. I just can't bring myself to walk through those doors and see her empty spot in the alto section. She always stood right behind me, second row on the left. Sometimes she'd tap me on the shoulder if we were supposed to stand and I hadn't noticed the director's cue. So, no, I haven't been singing either. \n\nI suppose the long and short of it is... no. No, doctor, I really can't think of a single thing that I'm actually finding pleasure in right now. I just go through the motions of the day, making my meals, washing the dishes, checking the mail, but it's all just... flat. Everything is just so flat and gray. It's like I'm just waiting for the day to be over so I can go to sleep, but then I wake up the next morning and it's just the same flat, gray routine all over again. I just don't know how to get the color back into things.\n\nDoctor: Have you been avoiding social interactions or events that you would normally attend?\n\nPatient: Well, yes. Yes, I suppose I have been. It's just... ever since my choir friend passed so suddenly, I really just haven't been myself at all. \n\nTake the church planning committee, for example. We meet on the second Tuesday of every month, usually in the fellowship hall, to go over the calendar and organize the upcoming events. I've been on that committee for, oh, it must be twelve years now, and I've started missing those meetings. I just can't bring myself to go, which is so unlike me—I never, ever would have missed those church planning things before. I was always the one leading the charge, making sure everything was running smoothly! \n\nBut now... well, the other day I was trying to look over the potluck sign-up sheets for the upcoming spring luncheon. Usually I love organizing that, making sure everyone is assigned a proper dish so we don't end up with five potato salads and absolutely no desserts. But I was just sitting there at my kitchen table, looking at the names, and I just started crying. Just weeping right over the potluck lists! It makes absolutely no sense, but the tears just wouldn't stop. \n\nAnd the phone calls, too. I used to handle all those coordination calls so easily, you know, people calling to ask if they should bring paper plates or if they need to come early to set up the folding chairs. It was second nature to me, I could chat and organize all afternoon. But now, the phone rings and I just get all worked up. My chest gets tight and I just stare at the caller ID until the answering machine finally picks up. I can't even bring myself to pick up the receiver to talk to people I've known for decades. So I just stay home. I stay home and I ignore the calls and I skip the meetings, because I just... I just can't face anyone right now. I don't even recognize myself behaving this way, hiding away from everyone, but I just don't have it in me to go out and pretend everything is normal.\n\nDoctor: Are you avoiding people or places that remind you of your friend?\n\nPatient: Avoiding places that remind me of her? Hmm... well, I'm not sure I'd say that, exactly. I know I mentioned the choir room earlier, and not wanting to see her empty spot in the alto section, but... outside of that, I haven't really noticed myself doing that. I mean, it's not like I'm purposely staying away from the places we used to go together just because they bring up memories. \n\nLike the little garden center down on Route 4, for instance. We used to go there every single spring to pick out our flats of impatiens and petunias. She always took so long deciding between the pinks and the purples, and I'd just be standing there with my cart, teasing her, telling her they all look exactly the same once they're in the ground! She was so particular about her flower beds. But I wouldn't avoid going to that nursery now just because it reminds me of her. If anything, those memories are quite dear to me. \n\nThe truth is, I'm just... I'm just not going anywhere at all. It's not the memories keeping me away from places, it's just this heavy feeling I have about absolutely everything. Like I was saying about the phone calls, I'm ignoring everybody, even people who didn't know her from Adam. The girl who does my hair, Betty, she called on Tuesday to remind me of my regular trim, and I just let it ring and ring. Betty didn't even know her, they never even crossed paths. And the mailman, I usually wave or say hello when he drops the letters in the box, but lately I just wait until his truck turns the corner before I even open the front door. \n\nSo, no, doctor, I don't think I'm running away from reminders of my friend. I think I'm just... well, I'm just sort of retreating from the whole world right now. Does that make sense? It's just too much trouble to put on a brave face and make small talk, no matter where I am or who I'm with, whether they remind me of her or not.\n\nDoctor: Are you having trouble taking care of your basic needs, like eating or bathing, since your friend passed away?\n\nPatient: Eating and bathing? Oh, heavens, no, I'm not... I mean, I'm still showering every morning. It's just part of the routine, you know, just going through the motions like I was saying before. And I'm eating, though it's mostly just a piece of toast or warming up a can of soup. I certainly don't have the energy to cook a full roast or anything elaborate, but I am making sure I'm fed and dressed. \n\nBut if you mean taking care of my actual life, my responsibilities... well, that's a whole different story. That's where things have really just completely fallen apart. \n\nI've actually had to let the other church members take over the coordination calls, the sign-up lists, and pretty much all the planning parts of the spring luncheon. I'm just not keeping up the way I always did before, and I finally had to admit it. And you have to understand, Doctor, I have run that spring luncheon for over a decade. I know exactly how many folding tables we need from the basement, I know that Mrs. Higgins needs to be seated near the aisle because of her walker, and I know exactly who makes the good casseroles and who tries to sneak in those dry, store-bought cookies. It was always my ship to steer! I took such pride in it. \n\nBut last week, I finally had to... well, actually I didn't even call, because like I said, I can't stand the phone right now. I had my husband drop off a note to Eleanor—she's the church secretary—and I told her that she and Mary would just have to take over the master lists and the phone tree. It honestly broke my heart to do it, truly it did, because Mary, bless her heart, is terribly disorganized. The last time she tried to help with a big event, she completely forgot to order the extra napkins and we had a terrible sticky mess when someone spilled the fruit punch. \n\nBut I just... I couldn't do it. The thought of sitting down with those lists and making sure the luncheon goes off without a hitch, it's just a mountain I cannot climb right now. I'm just not keeping up with my life. So I've just handed it all over to them, all my lists and my calls and my luncheon duties, which just goes to show you how out of sorts I really am. I never would have let Mary near those lists in a million years if I were in my right mind.\n\nDoctor: Are you spending most of your days alone at home?\n\nPatient: Alone? Well, I suppose that depends on how you look at it. I am at home, yes, I'm at home all day long, every single day. But I'm not entirely by myself, because my husband is there. He retired a few years back, so he's usually puttering around the house somewhere. He tries his best, bless his heart, he really does. He'll come into the living room and ask if I want to take a drive, or if I want to go with him to the grocery store just to get out of the house, but I just... I just stay right in my armchair. \n\nI used to be up and about from dawn till dusk, doing the laundry, dusting the baseboards, making sure the house was perfectly presentable in case anyone from the church dropped by. You know, I always kept a very tidy house, the kind where you could practically eat off the floors. But lately, I just sit in that chair in the corner by the front window. Arthur will be out in the garage tinkering with his tools, organizing his wrenches for the hundredth time, or he'll be in the den watching those old Westerns he loves so much, with the volume turned up entirely too loud because he absolutely refuses to get his hearing checked. I've told him a dozen times to go to the clinic, but you know how stubborn men can be about doctors. \n\nAnyway, so... physically, there is someone else under the roof with me. I'm not a hermit living out in the woods by myself. But I feel... I just feel completely isolated, even with him right there in the next room. We don't really talk much right now because I just don't have the words, and I think he's afraid of saying the wrong thing and making me cry again. So I'm just shut away in that house, not stepping foot outside the front door, not even to water the ferns on the porch. So I am home, yes, just letting the hours pass by in my slippers, but I wouldn't say I'm completely alone.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself constantly thinking about your friend and wishing she were still here with you?\n\nPatient: Constantly? Wishing she were here? Well... no, I wouldn't say constantly. It’s a strange thing, isn't it? You'd think I would be. Emotional pain? The intensity of it? Well, I... I really don't know how to answer that, Doctor, because I'm not sure I'd call it intense pain at all. 

You see, when you hear the words "intense emotional pain," you immediately think of those women in the movies, don't you? Or on those daytime soap operas. The ones who throw themselves over the casket, wailing and sobbing into their handkerchiefs, completely unable to even stand up on their own two feet. I remember when Arthur's cousin passed away—oh, it must be fifteen years ago now—his widow, Brenda, was exactly like that. She had to be physically held up by her two grown sons at the graveside service, just weeping and carrying on, completely inconsolable. And I suppose that's what true, intense emotional pain looks like. That sharp, stabbing agony that just tears you right down the middle.

But for me... I don't have that. I really don't. Like I was trying to explain just a moment ago with the Miller boy and the car... it's not a sharp feeling in my chest. It's not this unbearable, screaming agony. It's really just... nothing. A heavy, exhausting sort of nothing. 

I suppose if you're asking for a scale, like they do at the hospital when you go in for a procedure—you know, when the nurses ask "on a scale of one to ten, how bad is the pain?"—I wouldn't even know what number to give you. Because it doesn't feel like pain. It just feels like I've been completely hollowed out, like an old gourd. Arthur actually asked me the other evening if my heart was hurting, because I was just sitting there so quietly, and I had to tell him, "Arthur, I don't think my heart is doing much of anything at all right now." 

So, I really couldn't give you a description of intense pain. I just don't have that feeling to give you. It's just this terribly heavy numbness that won't go away.

Except maybe once, oh, years and years ago, over whether to use the blue hymnals or the red ones for the Christmas Eve service, but that was just us being silly. \n\nSo, no, I don't have any guilt weighing on my heart. I know I was a good friend to her and she was a wonderful friend to me. It's really just the... the sheer shock of it all. Just the absolute suddenness that I can't seem to wrap my head around. You just don't expect to be drinking coffee with someone one day and then... well, you just don't expect them to be gone. But no, no guilt. Just this awful, heavy sadness that won't lift.\n\nDoctor: Are there any activities that you still find pleasure in since your friend passed away?\n\nPatient: Oh, goodness, pleasure... well, I suppose that’s really what we were just talking about, isn't it? The gardening and the baking, those were my main things. And like I said, those are just completely gone for me right now. I just can't seem to muster up the energy or the... the joy for them. \n\nLet me think... is there anything else? Well, there's my evening television programs. Usually, I love watching those British mysteries, you know the ones, where it's a cozy little village and everyone knows everyone else's business, but then there's a murder and the local vicar or some little old lady has to solve it. My husband and I used to watch them together, and I kept the tradition going. I usually find them so comforting, trying to piece together the clues before the detective does. But lately... well, I turn the television on, right at eight o'clock, just like always. I sit in my usual chair with my cup of chamomile tea, and I look at the screen, but I'm not really watching it. The characters are talking, and I know they're solving a mystery, but I just can't follow the plot. My mind just wanders off, thinking about her, or just thinking about nothing at all, really. Just this sort of blank, heavy feeling. Before I know it, the hour is up, they've caught the killer, and I couldn't even tell you who it was or why they did it. \n\nAnd then there's the church choir, of course. Singing has always been such a huge part of my life. I'm a soprano, well, a second soprano these days, the high notes aren't quite what they used to be when I was in my thirties. But usually, Wednesday night practice is the highlight of my week. I love the harmonies, I love the fellowship, I love the way the music fills up the sanctuary. But since she passed... I haven't been back. I just can't bring myself to walk through those doors and see her empty spot in the alto section. She always stood right behind me, second row on the left. Sometimes she'd tap me on the shoulder if we were supposed to stand and I hadn't noticed the director's cue. So, no, I haven't been singing either. \n\nI suppose the long and short of it is... no. No, doctor, I really can't think of a single thing that I'm actually finding pleasure in right now. I just go through the motions of the day, making my meals, washing the dishes, checking the mail, but it's all just... flat. Everything is just so flat and gray. It's like I'm just waiting for the day to be over so I can go to sleep, but then I wake up the next morning and it's just the same flat, gray routine all over again. I just don't know how to get the color back into things.\n\nDoctor: Have you been avoiding social interactions or events that you would normally attend?\n\nPatient: Well, yes. Yes, I suppose I have been. It's just... ever since my choir friend passed so suddenly, I really just haven't been myself at all. \n\nTake the church planning committee, for example. We meet on the second Tuesday of every month, usually in the fellowship hall, to go over the calendar and organize the upcoming events. I've been on that committee for, oh, it must be twelve years now, and I've started missing those meetings. I just can't bring myself to go, which is so unlike me—I never, ever would have missed those church planning things before. I was always the one leading the charge, making sure everything was running smoothly! \n\nBut now... well, the other day I was trying to look over the potluck sign-up sheets for the upcoming spring luncheon. Usually I love organizing that, making sure everyone is assigned a proper dish so we don't end up with five potato salads and absolutely no desserts. But I was just sitting there at my kitchen table, looking at the names, and I just started crying. Just weeping right over the potluck lists! It makes absolutely no sense, but the tears just wouldn't stop. \n\nAnd the phone calls, too. I used to handle all those coordination calls so easily, you know, people calling to ask if they should bring paper plates or if they need to come early to set up the folding chairs. It was second nature to me, I could chat and organize all afternoon. But now, the phone rings and I just get all worked up. My chest gets tight and I just stare at the caller ID until the answering machine finally picks up. I can't even bring myself to pick up the receiver to talk to people I've known for decades. So I just stay home. I stay home and I ignore the calls and I skip the meetings, because I just... I just can't face anyone right now. I don't even recognize myself behaving this way, hiding away from everyone, but I just don't have it in me to go out and pretend everything is normal.\n\nDoctor: Are you avoiding people or places that remind you of your friend?\n\nPatient: Avoiding places that remind me of her? Hmm... well, I'm not sure I'd say that, exactly. I know I mentioned the choir room earlier, and not wanting to see her empty spot in the alto section, but... outside of that, I haven't really noticed myself doing that. I mean, it's not like I'm purposely staying away from the places we used to go together just because they bring up memories. \n\nLike the little garden center down on Route 4, for instance. We used to go there every single spring to pick out our flats of impatiens and petunias. She always took so long deciding between the pinks and the purples, and I'd just be standing there with my cart, teasing her, telling her they all look exactly the same once they're in the ground! She was so particular about her flower beds. But I wouldn't avoid going to that nursery now just because it reminds me of her. If anything, those memories are quite dear to me. \n\nThe truth is, I'm just... I'm just not going anywhere at all. It's not the memories keeping me away from places, it's just this heavy feeling I have about absolutely everything. Like I was saying about the phone calls, I'm ignoring everybody, even people who didn't know her from Adam. The girl who does my hair, Betty, she called on Tuesday to remind me of my regular trim, and I just let it ring and ring. Betty didn't even know her, they never even crossed paths. And the mailman, I usually wave or say hello when he drops the letters in the box, but lately I just wait until his truck turns the corner before I even open the front door. \n\nSo, no, doctor, I don't think I'm running away from reminders of my friend. I think I'm just... well, I'm just sort of retreating from the whole world right now. Does that make sense? It's just too much trouble to put on a brave face and make small talk, no matter where I am or who I'm with, whether they remind me of her or not.\n\nDoctor: Are you having trouble taking care of your basic needs, like eating or bathing, since your friend passed away?\n\nPatient: Eating and bathing? Oh, heavens, no, I'm not... I mean, I'm still showering every morning. It's just part of the routine, you know, just going through the motions like I was saying before. And I'm eating, though it's mostly just a piece of toast or warming up a can of soup. I certainly don't have the energy to cook a full roast or anything elaborate, but I am making sure I'm fed and dressed. \n\nBut if you mean taking care of my actual life, my responsibilities... well, that's a whole different story. That's where things have really just completely fallen apart. \n\nI've actually had to let the other church members take over the coordination calls, the sign-up lists, and pretty much all the planning parts of the spring luncheon. I'm just not keeping up the way I always did before, and I finally had to admit it. And you have to understand, Doctor, I have run that spring luncheon for over a decade. I know exactly how many folding tables we need from the basement, I know that Mrs. Higgins needs to be seated near the aisle because of her walker, and I know exactly who makes the good casseroles and who tries to sneak in those dry, store-bought cookies. It was always my ship to steer! I took such pride in it. \n\nBut last week, I finally had to... well, actually I didn't even call, because like I said, I can't stand the phone right now. I had my husband drop off a note to Eleanor—she's the church secretary—and I told her that she and Mary would just have to take over the master lists and the phone tree. It honestly broke my heart to do it, truly it did, because Mary, bless her heart, is terribly disorganized. The last time she tried to help with a big event, she completely forgot to order the extra napkins and we had a terrible sticky mess when someone spilled the fruit punch. \n\nBut I just... I couldn't do it. The thought of sitting down with those lists and making sure the luncheon goes off without a hitch, it's just a mountain I cannot climb right now. I'm just not keeping up with my life. So I've just handed it all over to them, all my lists and my calls and my luncheon duties, which just goes to show you how out of sorts I really am. I never would have let Mary near those lists in a million years if I were in my right mind.\n\nDoctor: Are you spending most of your days alone at home?\n\nPatient: Alone? Well, I suppose that depends on how you look at it. I am at home, yes, I'm at home all day long, every single day. But I'm not entirely by myself, because my husband is there. He retired a few years back, so he's usually puttering around the house somewhere. He tries his best, bless his heart, he really does. He'll come into the living room and ask if I want to take a drive, or if I want to go with him to the grocery store just to get out of the house, but I just... I just stay right in my armchair. \n\nI used to be up and about from dawn till dusk, doing the laundry, dusting the baseboards, making sure the house was perfectly presentable in case anyone from the church dropped by. You know, I always kept a very tidy house, the kind where you could practically eat off the floors. But lately, I just sit in that chair in the corner by the front window. Arthur will be out in the garage tinkering with his tools, organizing his wrenches for the hundredth time, or he'll be in the den watching those old Westerns he loves so much, with the volume turned up entirely too loud because he absolutely refuses to get his hearing checked. I've told him a dozen times to go to the clinic, but you know how stubborn men can be about doctors. \n\nAnyway, so... physically, there is someone else under the roof with me. I'm not a hermit living out in the woods by myself. But I feel... I just feel completely isolated, even with him right there in the next room. We don't really talk much right now because I just don't have the words, and I think he's afraid of saying the wrong thing and making me cry again. So I'm just shut away in that house, not stepping foot outside the front door, not even to water the ferns on the porch. So I am home, yes, just letting the hours pass by in my slippers, but I wouldn't say I'm completely alone.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself constantly thinking about your friend and wishing she were still here with you?\n\nPatient: Constantly? Wishing she were here? Well... no, I wouldn't say constantly. It’s a strange thing, isn't it? You'd think I would be. You'd think I'd be sitting there in my chair replaying all our old conversations or crying over photographs, just wishing she could walk through the front door and tell me all about what her grandchildren are up to. But... honestly, my mind is just sort of... blank most of the time. \n\nIt's like a television set that's been unplugged. I sit in that armchair I told you about, the one by the front window, and I just stare out at the street. Yesterday, I must have watched the Miller boy down the block—he's a teenager now, just got his learner's permit—I watched him try to parallel park his mother's Buick for what felt like an absolute eternity. He just kept bumping the curb, over and over, pulling out, backing in, bumping the curb again. And I just sat there and watched him do it. I wasn't thinking about my friend while I was watching. I wasn't really thinking about anything at all. \n\nIt's just this terrible flatness. So, no, I'm not consumed with thoughts of her every waking second. It's not this sharp, piercing pain of missing her all day long, it's more like... well, like all the color has just been washed out of the room, and it takes entirely too much effort to even form a thought about why. Does that make sense? I just feel so completely drained that I don't even have the energy to actively wish for things to be different anymore. I'm just sitting there, letting the clock tick.\n\nDoctor: How would you describe the intensity of your emotional pain since your friend passed away?\n\nPatient: Emotional pain? The intensity of it? Well, I... I really don't know how to answer that, Doctor, because I'm not sure I'd call it intense pain at all. \n\nYou see, when you hear the words \"intense emotional pain,\" you immediately think of those women in the movies, don't you? Or on those daytime soap operas. The ones who throw themselves over the casket, wailing and sobbing into their handkerchiefs, completely unable to even stand up on their own two feet. I remember when Arthur's cousin passed away—oh, it must be fifteen years ago now—his widow, Brenda, was exactly like that. She had to be physically held up by her two grown sons at the graveside service, just weeping and carrying on, completely inconsolable. A heavy, exhausting sort of nothing. \n\nI suppose if you're asking for a scale, like they do at the hospital when you go in for a procedure—you know, when the nurses ask \"on a scale of one to ten, how bad is the pain?\"—I wouldn't even know what number to give you. Sad? Well, I... I don't know if "sad" is really the right word for it. But lately... well, I'll go out there with my shears, and I just stand there looking at them. I'll clip one or two stems, and then I just feel this heavy sigh come over me, and I put the shears right back in the bucket and go inside. It just doesn't bring me that little spark of joy it usually does. \n\nAnd it's the same with my baking. I've always been the one to bake the communion bread—the recipe with the honey and the whole wheat, everyone says it's much better than those little wafers. I usually love the whole process, the kneading and the rising, the smell filling up the kitchen. But last week, when it was my turn, I just bought a couple of loaves from the bakery down the street. I couldn't even bring myself to pull the flour out of the pantry. I just sat in the kitchen staring at the mixing bowl, feeling completely empty. It's like all the color has just drained out of everything I used to love doing. I just don't have the heart for any of it right now.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel guilty about anything related to your friend's death?\n\nPatient: Guilty? Oh, goodness, no... no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I know sometimes people get all tangled up in knots when someone passes, thinking, oh, I should have called more, or I should have noticed something was wrong, or maybe they had a fight they never resolved. But with us... well, we saw each other just about every single week. Every Sunday for service, and Wednesdays for practice, regular as clockwork. \n\nThe very last time I saw her, right before it happened, we were just standing by the fellowship hall coffee urn, and she was telling me all about her granddaughter's upcoming recital—she plays the flute, you know, such a sweet, talented little girl—and she looked perfectly fine. Not a care in the world. And then... well, her daughter told me it was just peaceful, in her sleep. Her heart just stopped. So there wasn't anything anyone could have done. It wasn't like she was laid up in the hospital and I forgot to visit, or we'd had some silly falling out. We never, ever argued. Not in fifteen years! Except maybe once, oh, years and years ago, over whether to use the blue hymnals or the red ones for the Christmas Eve service, but that was just us being silly. \n\nSo, no, I don't have any guilt weighing on my heart. I know I was a good friend to her and she was a wonderful friend to me. It's really just the... the sheer shock of it all. Just the absolute suddenness that I can't seem to wrap my head around. You just don't expect to be drinking coffee with someone one day and then... well, you just don't expect them to be gone. But no, no guilt. Just this awful, heavy sadness that won't lift.\n\nDoctor: Are there any activities that you still find pleasure in since your friend passed away?\n\nPatient: Oh, goodness, pleasure... well, I suppose that’s really what we were just talking about, isn't it? The gardening and the baking, those were my main things. And like I said, those are just completely gone for me right now. I just can't seem to muster up the energy or the... the joy for them. \n\nLet me think... is there anything else? Well, there's my evening television programs. Usually, I love watching those British mysteries, you know the ones, where it's a cozy little village and everyone knows everyone else's business, but then there's a murder and the local vicar or some little old lady has to solve it. My husband and I used to watch them together, and I kept the tradition going. I usually find them so comforting, trying to piece together the clues before the detective does. But lately... well, I turn the television on, right at eight o'clock, just like always. I sit in my usual chair with my cup of chamomile tea, and I look at the screen, but I'm not really watching it. The characters are talking, and I know they're solving a mystery, but I just can't follow the plot. My mind just wanders off, thinking about her, or just thinking about nothing at all, really. Just this sort of blank, heavy feeling. Before I know it, the hour is up, they've caught the killer, and I couldn't even tell you who it was or why they did it. \n\nAnd then there's the church choir, of course. Singing has always been such a huge part of my life. I'm a soprano, well, a second soprano these days, the high notes aren't quite what they used to be when I was in my thirties. But usually, Wednesday night practice is the highlight of my week. I love the harmonies, I love the fellowship, I love the way the music fills up the sanctuary. But since she passed... I haven't been back. I just can't bring myself to walk through those doors and see her empty spot in the alto section. She always stood right behind me, second row on the left. Sometimes she'd tap me on the shoulder if we were supposed to stand and I hadn't noticed the director's cue. So, no, I haven't been singing either. \n\nI suppose the long and short of it is... no. No, doctor, I really can't think of a single thing that I'm actually finding pleasure in right now. I just go through the motions of the day, making my meals, washing the dishes, checking the mail, but it's all just... flat. Everything is just so flat and gray. It's like I'm just waiting for the day to be over so I can go to sleep, but then I wake up the next morning and it's just the same flat, gray routine all over again. I just don't know how to get the color back into things.\n\nDoctor: Have you been avoiding social interactions or events that you would normally attend?\n\nPatient: Well, yes. Yes, I suppose I have been. It's just... ever since my choir friend passed so suddenly, I really just haven't been myself at all. \n\nTake the church planning committee, for example. We meet on the second Tuesday of every month, usually in the fellowship hall, to go over the calendar and organize the upcoming events. I've been on that committee for, oh, it must be twelve years now, and I've started missing those meetings. I just can't bring myself to go, which is so unlike me—I never, ever would have missed those church planning things before. I was always the one leading the charge, making sure everything was running smoothly! \n\nBut now... well, the other day I was trying to look over the potluck sign-up sheets for the upcoming spring luncheon. Usually I love organizing that, making sure everyone is assigned a proper dish so we don't end up with five potato salads and absolutely no desserts. But I was just sitting there at my kitchen table, looking at the names, and I just started crying. Just weeping right over the potluck lists! It makes absolutely no sense, but the tears just wouldn't stop. \n\nAnd the phone calls, too. I used to handle all those coordination calls so easily, you know, people calling to ask if they should bring paper plates or if they need to come early to set up the folding chairs. It was second nature to me, I could chat and organize all afternoon. But now, the phone rings and I just get all worked up. My chest gets tight and I just stare at the caller ID until the answering machine finally picks up. I can't even bring myself to pick up the receiver to talk to people I've known for decades. So I just stay home. I stay home and I ignore the calls and I skip the meetings, because I just... I just can't face anyone right now. I don't even recognize myself behaving this way, hiding away from everyone, but I just don't have it in me to go out and pretend everything is normal.\n\nDoctor: Are you avoiding people or places that remind you of your friend?\n\nPatient: Avoiding places that remind me of her? Hmm... well, I'm not sure I'd say that, exactly. I know I mentioned the choir room earlier, and not wanting to see her empty spot in the alto section, but... outside of that, I haven't really noticed myself doing that. I mean, it's not like I'm purposely staying away from the places we used to go together just because they bring up memories. \n\nLike the little garden center down on Route 4, for instance. We used to go there every single spring to pick out our flats of impatiens and petunias. She always took so long deciding between the pinks and the purples, and I'd just be standing there with my cart, teasing her, telling her they all look exactly the same once they're in the ground! I think I'm just... well, I'm just sort of retreating from the whole world right now. Does that make sense? I know exactly how many folding tables we need from the basement, I know that Mrs. Higgins needs to be seated near the aisle because of her walker, and I know exactly who makes the good casseroles and who tries to sneak in those dry, store-bought cookies. I had my husband drop off a note to Eleanor—she's the church secretary—and I told her that she and Mary would just have to take over the master lists and the phone tree. It honestly broke my heart to do it, truly it did, because Mary, bless her heart, is terribly disorganized. The last time she tried to help with a big event, she completely forgot to order the extra napkins and we had a terrible sticky mess when someone spilled the fruit punch. \n\nBut I just... I just don't have that feeling to give you. It's just this terribly heavy numbness that won't go away.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel sad most of the time since your friend passed away?\n\nPatient: Sad? ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Interested in things? Well, I suppose... I mean, I haven't really noticed a change in my interests, per se. It's not like I've suddenly decided I hate the things I used to love, or that I'm turning my nose up at my usual hobbies. 

Take my gardening, for instance. You know, I have always loved my garden. Arthur and I put in these beautiful raised beds out back—oh, it must have been five or six years ago now. And I still think about the garden. I still look out the kitchen window while I'm waiting for the kettle to boil, and I look at those cedar boxes, and I know that I should be getting the seedlings started indoors right about now if I want to have a decent crop of beefsteaks by August. 

So the interest is still there, I suppose. I haven't lost the knowledge of it, or the appreciation for a good, sturdy tomato plant. It's just that... well, like I was saying about the energy. I look at the garden, and I know I'm interested in it, but the thought of actually putting on my gardening clogs, finding my gloves—the good leather ones, not the cheap cotton ones that always get holes in the thumbs—and walking out there to actually dig in the dirt... it just feels like trying to wade through wet cement. 

So, no, I wouldn't say I've lost interest. It's not that I don't care about the garden, or my knitting, or the crossword puzzles I usually do on Sunday mornings. It's just that I can't seem to make myself actually do them. The interest is sitting right there where it always was, but I'm just too... blank... to reach out and pick it up. Does that make sense? I haven't stopped liking things, I just... I'm just sitting here instead.

Accept it and move on? Well, I... I really don't know how to answer that, Doctor. I honestly don't. 

When you say "accept it," it almost makes it sound like a package being delivered, doesn't it? Like the postman comes up to your front porch—our postman, Gary, he’s been doing our route for at least twelve years now, always wears those little blue shorts even when it gets awfully brisk in November—but it's like Gary comes to the door, hands you a heavy box, and you just sign your name on his little electronic pad and say, "Yes, thank you, I accept this." But this isn't a package. I can't just sign for it and put it on the hallway table and go about my day. 

And as for moving on... well, where exactly am I supposed to move on to? People use that phrase all the time, like you're just packing up the car and driving to a new town. But I'm right here. Like I was saying about that terrible blankness, I'm just sitting here. 

Arthur actually brought up something similar just yesterday morning over breakfast. He was pouring his coffee—he always uses that old blue mug with the chip on the handle that I've been trying to throw away since 2018—and he asked me what we were going to do about the summer vacation this year. Because usually, the four of us... Arthur and me, and her and her husband... we would always rent this little cabin up by the lake. We’ve been getting the exact same one, cabin number four with the green shutters and the screened-in porch, for years and years. And Arthur asked if we should still go, or if we should try going somewhere else to "move forward." 

I just looked at him, Doctor, and I didn't have a single word to say. I couldn't even picture the summer. I can't picture next week. When I try to look ahead to moving on, or getting back to normal, or whatever you want to call it... there's just a wall of fog. I can't see through it. 

So if you're asking me if I think I'll ever be able to accept it and move on... I really don't know. I can't see that far ahead to tell you. I'm just stuck right here in this heavy sort of nothing, and I don't know if it will ever change. I really couldn't say.

Does that make sense? I just feel so completely drained that I don't even have the energy to actively wish for things to be different anymore. I've told him a dozen times to go to the clinic, but you know how stubborn men can be about doctors. \n\nAnyway, so... physically, there is someone else under the roof with me. I'm not a hermit living out in the woods by myself. But I feel... I just feel completely isolated, even with him right there in the next room. We don't really talk much right now because I just don't have the words, and I think he's afraid of saying the wrong thing and making me cry again. So I'm just shut away in that house, not stepping foot outside the front door, not even to water the ferns on the porch. So I am home, yes, just letting the hours pass by in my slippers, but I wouldn't say I'm completely alone.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself constantly thinking about your friend and wishing she were still here with you?\n\nPatient: Constantly? Wishing she were here? Well... no, I wouldn't say constantly. It’s a strange thing, isn't it? You'd think I would be. You'd think I'd be sitting there in my chair replaying all our old conversations or crying over photographs, just wishing she could walk through the front door and tell me all about what her grandchildren are up to. But... honestly, my mind is just sort of... blank most of the time. \n\nIt's like a television set that's been unplugged. I sit in that armchair I told you about, the one by the front window, and I just stare out at the street. Yesterday, I must have watched the Miller boy down the block—he's a teenager now, just got his learner's permit—I watched him try to parallel park his mother's Buick for what felt like an absolute eternity. He just kept bumping the curb, over and over, pulling out, backing in, bumping the curb again. And I just sat there and watched him do it. I wasn't thinking about my friend while I was watching. I wasn't really thinking about anything at all. \n\nIt's just this terrible flatness. So, no, I'm not consumed with thoughts of her every waking second. It's not this sharp, piercing pain of missing her all day long, it's more like... well, like all the color has just been washed out of the room, and it takes entirely too much effort to even form a thought about why. Does that make sense? I just feel so completely drained that I don't even have the energy to actively wish for things to be different anymore. I'm just sitting there, letting the clock tick.\n\nDoctor: How would you describe the intensity of your emotional pain since your friend passed away?\n\nPatient: Emotional pain? The intensity of it? Well, I... I really don't know how to answer that, Doctor, because I'm not sure I'd call it intense pain at all. \n\nYou see, when you hear the words \"intense emotional pain,\" you immediately think of those women in the movies, don't you? Or on those daytime soap operas. The ones who throw themselves over the casket, wailing and sobbing into their handkerchiefs, completely unable to even stand up on their own two feet. I remember when Arthur's cousin passed away—oh, it must be fifteen years ago now—his widow, Brenda, was exactly like that. She had to be physically held up by her two grown sons at the graveside service, just weeping and carrying on, completely inconsolable. And I suppose that's what true, intense emotional pain looks like. That sharp, stabbing agony that just tears you right down the middle.\n\nBut for me... I don't have that. I really don't. Like I was trying to explain just a moment ago with the Miller boy and the car... it's not a sharp feeling in my chest. It's not this unbearable, screaming agony. It's really just... nothing. A heavy, exhausting sort of nothing. \n\nI suppose if you're asking for a scale, like they do at the hospital when you go in for a procedure—you know, when the nurses ask \"on a scale of one to ten, how bad is the pain?\"—I wouldn't even know what number to give you. Because it doesn't feel like pain. It just feels like I've been completely hollowed out, like an old gourd. Arthur actually asked me the other evening if my heart was hurting, because I was just sitting there so quietly, and I had to tell him, \"Arthur, I don't think my heart is doing much of anything at all right now.\" \n\nSo, I really couldn't give you a description of intense pain. I just don't have that feeling to give you. It's just this terribly heavy numbness that won't go away.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel sad most of the time since your friend passed away?\n\nPatient: Sad? Well, I... I don't know if \"sad\" is really the right word for it. When I think of being sad, I think of... oh, well, like when Arthur's old golden retriever, Buster, had to be put to sleep back in... oh, it must have been 1998. Yes, 1998. Arthur was just absolutely devastated, of course, and I was terribly sad then, too. I remember we both cried for days, and I couldn't even look at Buster's little plaid dog bed by the fireplace without getting this awful, thick lump in my throat. That was sadness. You know, that heavy, aching feeling where you just want to have a good long cry into a tissue.\n\nBut this? Since she passed? It's not that weepy, blue kind of sadness at all. Pastor Thomas from our church actually came by just this past Tuesday—or wait, was it Wednesday? No, it was Tuesday, because I remember hearing the garbage trucks backing up down the street while he was on the porch. Anyway, he brought over a tuna noodle casserole, which was very thoughtful, bless his heart, even though Arthur absolutely refuses to eat peas and of course it was full of them. But Pastor Thomas sat down on the sofa, held my hand, and asked me almost the exact same thing you just did. He asked if I was drowning in sorrow. And I had to look him right in the eye and say, \"Pastor, I'm not drowning in anything. The pool is completely dry.\" \n\nSo, no, I wouldn't say I feel sad most of the time. It's just... well, like I was trying to explain before, it's just this total blankness. Being sad almost feels like it would require a certain amount of energy, you know? Like you have to actively feel the sadness, you have to muster up the tears. And I just don't have the energy for it. I don't sit in my chair feeling blue, I just... sit there. So I really couldn't say I feel sad, no.\n\nDoctor: Are you finding it harder to feel interested in things you used to enjoy?\n\nPatient: Interested in things? Well, I suppose... I mean, I haven't really noticed a change in my interests, per se. It's not like I've suddenly decided I hate the things I used to love, or that I'm turning my nose up at my usual hobbies. \n\nTake my gardening, for instance. You know, I have always loved my garden. Arthur and I put in these beautiful raised beds out back—oh, it must have been five or six years ago now. We used cedar, because cedar resists rot so much better than pine, and Arthur was very particular about making sure the corners were perfectly square. I usually spend hours out there in the spring, getting the soil turned over, planning out where the tomatoes will go so they get the morning sun but not the harsh afternoon heat, making sure the marigolds are planted around the perimeter to keep the rabbits away. And I still think about the garden. I still look out the kitchen window while I'm waiting for the kettle to boil, and I look at those cedar boxes, and I know that I should be getting the seedlings started indoors right about now if I want to have a decent crop of beefsteaks by August. \n\nSo the interest is still there, I suppose. I haven't lost the knowledge of it, or the appreciation for a good, sturdy tomato plant. It's just that... well, like I was saying about the energy. I look at the garden, and I know I'm interested in it, but the thought of actually putting on my gardening clogs, finding my gloves—the good leather ones, not the cheap cotton ones that always get holes in the thumbs—and walking out there to actually dig in the dirt... it just feels like trying to wade through wet cement. \n\nSo, no, I wouldn't say I've lost interest. It's not that I don't care about the garden, or my knitting, or the crossword puzzles I usually do on Sunday mornings. It's just that I can't seem to make myself actually do them. The interest is sitting right there where it always was, but I'm just too... blank... to reach out and pick it up. Does that make sense? I haven't stopped liking things, I just... I'm just sitting here instead.\n\nDoctor: Do you think you would ever be able to accept your friend's death and move on with your life?\n\nPatient: Accept it and move on? Well, I... I really don't know how to answer that, Doctor. I honestly don't. \n\nWhen you say \"accept it,\" it almost makes it sound like a package being delivered, doesn't it? Like the postman comes up to your front porch—our postman, Gary, he’s been doing our route for at least twelve years now, always wears those little blue shorts even when it gets awfully brisk in November—but it's like Gary comes to the door, hands you a heavy box, and you just sign your name on his little electronic pad and say, \"Yes, thank you, I accept this.\" But this isn't a package. I can't just sign for it and put it on the hallway table and go about my day. \n\nAnd as for moving on... well, where exactly am I supposed to move on to? People use that phrase all the time, like you're just packing up the car and driving to a new town. But I'm right here. Like I was saying about that terrible blankness, I'm just sitting here. \n\nArthur actually brought up something similar just yesterday morning over breakfast. He was pouring his coffee—he always uses that old blue mug with the chip on the handle that I've been trying to throw away since 2018—and he asked me what we were going to do about the summer vacation this year. Because usually, the four of us... Arthur and me, and her and her husband... we would always rent this little cabin up by the lake. We’ve been getting the exact same one, cabin number four with the green shutters and the screened-in porch, for years and years. And Arthur asked if we should still go, or if we should try going somewhere else to \"move forward.\" \n\nI just looked at him, Doctor, and I didn't have a single word to say. I couldn't even picture the summer. I can't picture next week. When I try to look ahead to moving on, or getting back to normal, or whatever you want to call it... there's just a wall of fog. I can't see through it. \n\nSo if you're asking me if I think I'll ever be able to accept it and move on... I really don't know. I can't see that far ahead to tell you. I'm just stuck right here in this heavy sort of nothing, and I don't know if it will ever change. I really couldn't say.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you've lost interest in activities you used to enjoy?\n\nPatient: Oh, well... didn't we just... I feel like we just went over this, Doctor. About the garden and the tomatoes? Like I was trying to explain just a few minutes ago, it’s really not a matter of losing interest. I haven't lost my interest in things at all. \n\nI mentioned my knitting earlier, didn't I? Well, just to give you another example, I have this beautiful, incredibly soft alpaca yarn sitting in a wicker basket right next to my armchair in the living room. It's a lovely shade of periwinkle blue, and I bought it specifically to make a little cardigan for my niece's baby shower. She's expecting her second in late October, a little girl this time, which is just wonderful since they already have a boy, little Michael. Anyway, I look at that periwinkle yarn every single day, and I still think, 'Oh, I really want to see how that lace stitch pattern turns out.' The interest is absolutely still there. I still care about how the cardigan will look, just like I still care about the beefsteak tomatoes and the Sunday crosswords. \n\nIt's just that I sit in my armchair, and I stare at the basket, and I just... can't bring myself to pick up the knitting needles. I just sit there looking at it. So, no, I really wouldn't say the interest itself is gone. It's just exactly like I said a minute ago, I'm just too blank to actually do any of it right now.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like a part of you has died along with your friend?\n\nPatient: A part of me died? Oh... no, I really don't think I would say that. That sounds awfully dramatic, doesn't it? Like something out of one of those daytime soap operas. My sister-in-law, Brenda—Arthur's sister, she lives over in Springfield—she watches those programs religiously. Has since the late eighties, I think. She's always talking about characters losing a piece of their soul and all that sort of thing. But no, I don't feel like a piece of me is dead. \n\nI'm still very much here. I know I'm still me. I was actually just looking in the hallway mirror this morning—it's this lovely oval mirror with a heavy brass frame that Arthur's mother left us when she passed away, bless her heart, it has these delicate little etched vines all around the edges. Anyway, I was looking in it while I was trying to decide if I had the energy to put on a bit of lipstick. I didn't, in the end, I just couldn't see the point of it. But I looked at my face, and it's the same face. I have all the same memories, the same thoughts. I still remember every single detail of the time she and I took a ceramics class together down at the community center. Oh, that must have been twenty years ago at least. I made this terribly lopsided bowl that Arthur still uses for his loose change on his dresser, and she made a beautiful tall vase that she painted with little yellow daisies. \n\nSo, all of those pieces of me, the memories and the person I've always been... they haven't gone anywhere. They certainly haven't died. They're still right here inside me. It's just... well, it goes right back to what I was saying before about that heavy nothingness. I'm still entirely me, every single part of me is alive and intact. I'm just a me who is sitting in a thick fog, staring at a basket of periwinkle yarn. I haven't lost a piece of myself, Doctor. Periods where I felt a little better? Oh... no, I really haven't. Not even for a moment, honestly. It's just been one long, flat stretch since she passed. 

I know some people say that grief comes in waves, you know? My neighbor, Mrs. Gable—she lives in the pale yellow house on the corner with the gorgeous hydrangeas out front—she told me when her husband passed, she would have moments where she could laugh at a memory or enjoy a cup of tea, and then the sadness would wash back over her. She said it was like standing in the ocean. But it hasn't been like that for me at all. There are no waves, no moments of relief where the sun peeks through the clouds, nothing like that. 

Just yesterday, Arthur tried to cheer me up. He went all the way down to that little bakery on Main Street, the one with the striped awning that smells like cinnamon the second you open the door, and he bought me a slice of their lemon pound cake. It's always been my absolute favorite, especially with a hot cup of Earl Grey. He brought it to me on one of our good china plates, the ones with the little pink rosebuds, and he looked so hopeful. And I took a bite, and... nothing. It just tasted like dust. I couldn't even muster up a smile for him, poor Arthur. He tries so hard. But no, Doctor, there haven't been any moments where the fog lifts. It's just been this constant, heavy blankness every single minute since the funeral. I just wake up, sit in the armchair, look at the knitting basket, and wait for the day to be over. It never really changes or gets any lighter.

But usually, Wednesday night practice is the highlight of my week. I love the harmonies, I love the fellowship, I love the way the music fills up the sanctuary. But since she passed... I haven't been back. I just can't bring myself to walk through those doors and see her empty spot in the alto section. She always stood right behind me, second row on the left. It's like I'm just waiting for the day to be over so I can go to sleep, but then I wake up the next morning and it's just the same flat, gray routine all over again. I just don't know how to get the color back into things.\n\nDoctor: Have you been avoiding social interactions or events that you would normally attend?\n\nPatient: Well, yes.
